Lessons.Title: Different Partial Quotients PLC Activity
ExplanationParagraphs: Original IM 2021 G5 U04:L11 Different Partial Quotients PLC Activity compares multiple valid decompositions of WHOLE-NUMBER DIVISION by a two-digit divisor, including sets of quotient chunks and metacognitive choice of a useful first multiple. The sum of selected partial QUOTIENTS must equal the full quotient, and corresponding products must partition the ORIGINAL dividend.

Warm-up Notice and Wonder Ways to Record: source 364÷13=28 is recorded through Clare/Jada different decompositions. Source examples include 13×10=130,13×20=260,13×5=65,13×3=39; 260+65+39=364 and partial quotients 20+5+3=28. A source figure may also present 130+130+65+39=364. Teacher reviews actual partial-quotient records rather than assuming a unique order.

Activity 1 Division Expressions: original source card activity targets 308÷14=22. Learners select an actual set of expressions whose partial QUOTIENTS add to 22 and whose dividend chunks sum to 308, leaving zero. Actual original option card deck is not independently verified; do not claim invented card expressions are publisher originals. Correct independent example 14×20=280 then14×2=28.

Activity 2 Choose Your Own Partial Quotients: source exercises 360÷15=24 (e.g. 300÷15=20 and60÷15=4), 945÷45=21 (900÷45=20 and45÷45=1) and 992÷31=32 (e.g. 31×30=930 and62÷31=2). Teacher asks children to choose a first useful partial quotient, compare possible start values and revise when needed. Some source card expressions such as 341÷31=11 are helper chunks, not full 992÷31.

Exact selected Practice covers verified source quotients and helper chunks only. Teacher reviews card selection, original source diagram interpretation, complete remainder zero and partner explanations. Edulytiks independent teacher Cool-down 672÷24=28 does not recreate the publisher gated original.

Source and assessment limits: independently authored Edulytiks Cool-down with teacher-reviewed drawing/explanation. Original publisher gated Cool-down, standalone student PDF and original image binaries are not individually certified. KeyConcepts.Title: Partial quotient is a counted group
KeyConcepts.Definition: A partial quotient counts a portion of the final equal-sized groups.
KeyConcepts.Rule: If 320÷16=20, then 20 full groups of 16 consume 320.

KeyConcepts.Title: Several correct decompositions
KeyConcepts.Definition: Different sums of divisor-multiples can reconstruct the same dividend.

KeyConcepts.Title: Choose an efficient chunk
KeyConcepts.Definition: A larger convenient multiple can reduce the number of subtraction steps without changing the quotient.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Assume the only correct route is the shortest list
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Valid smaller partial chunks are acceptable if they cover the dividend exactly.

CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: A correct-looking sum can mask omitted or duplicated dividend pieces.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Multiply each selected partial quotient by the divisor and sum to the original dividend.

Lessons.Title: An Algorithm Using Partial Quotients
ExplanationParagraphs: Original IM 2021 G5 U04:L12 An Algorithm Using Partial Quotients: the source pupils read and complete a STACKED written division layout where each subtraction records a multiple of the divisor, and the full quotient is the SUM of the written partial quotients. Remainders and units of each partial step matter.

Warm-up Notice and Wonder Incomplete Solution: source begins 448÷16 and a first written 20 groups ×16=320, leaving 128, with a hint 5×16=80. Learners discuss what comes next, not simply quote a complete 28. The source asks teacher-led interpretation of the visual stacked layout.

Activity 1 Elena's Work: the actual source 448÷16=28, with partial 20,5,3: subtract 320 then80 then48 to reach zero; quotient 20+5+3=28. Label what each subtraction means and explain why 16 is the fixed divisor throughout.

Activity 2 Complete the Solution: source 492÷12 has 20×12=240 then another20×12=240 then remainder12; final 1×12=12 gives 41. Source 630÷15 begins 40×15=600 then30 remain, 2×15=30 so quotient42. The original student-facing third diagram appears only as a caption in teacher HTML and is not independently reconstructed; do not manufacture a third official quotient. Teacher reviews the actual page images and algorithm steps.

Exact digital Practice validates the known quotient and partial chunks. Original stack diagrams, intermediate quotient choice, explanations and unrecovered third source figure remain TEACHER_REVIEW_REQUIRED. Independently authored Cool-down uses 784÷28=28, rather than gated publisher Cool-down.

KeyConcepts.Title: Partial quotient recording
KeyConcepts.Definition: A division algorithm may repeatedly subtract whole multiples of a divisor while recording group counts.

KeyConcepts.Title: Remaining dividend
KeyConcepts.Definition: The remainder at each step is how much of the original dividend is not yet allocated.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Continue subtracting valid divisor multiples until remaining is below divisor.

KeyConcepts.Title: Multiplication verifies division
KeyConcepts.Definition: A quotient q with remainder r must satisfy divisor×q+r=dividend and 0≤r<divisor.
KeyConcepts.Example: A remainder of 42 with divisor 21 is not final.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Subtract the quotient count rather than the product
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Subtracting '20' directly is incorrect when 20 groups each have 21 items.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Compute 20×21=420 and subtract that from the dividend.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Stop with a remainder greater than or equal to divisor
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Another full group can still be removed if enough quantity remains.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Continue until the final whole-number remainder is smaller than the divisor.

CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Original source diagrams explicitly show Elena's 448÷16 and two incomplete stacks; invented numbers fail source parity.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Restore all verified source stacked subtractions; keep previous invented but valid examples only as extensions.

Lessons.Title: Divide Using Partial Quotients
ExplanationParagraphs: Original IM 2021 Grade5 U04:L13 Divide Using Partial Quotients: estimate quotient magnitude before a written partial-quotients algorithm, decide a convenient divisor multiple, compare partner strategies and justify that all quotient chunks together exactly account for the dividend.

Warm-up original Number Talk Divide: 110÷10=11,121÷11=11,132÷12=11,154÷14=11. Notice four changing dividends and divisors with a constant quotient eleven. Verify multiplication inverse, rather than relying on source images.

Activity 1 Compare Solutions: original Student Facing specifies Partner 1/2 division layouts and comparison with another group. The locally available teacher HTML does not reveal the numerical values in those embedded partner images, so no invented 672÷28 is represented as an official source problem. Use teacher-provided actual images or clearly independently authored examples for comparison, and assess students' selection of useful partial quotient chunks.

Activity 2 Estimate and Solve actual source: estimate and calculate 612÷34=18 (e.g. 34×10=340 and34×8=272); 529÷23=23 (23×20=460 and23×3=69); 1044÷29=36 (29×30=870 and29×6=174). Estimation benchmarks may be 600÷30≈20,500÷25≈20,1000÷30≈33; they are approximate guides, not unique mandated source answers.

Source partner card alignment, estimate arguments and full original vertical division records need TEACHER_REVIEW_REQUIRED. Exact source quotient choices cover only automatic subskills. Existing 672÷28,988÷38 examples are correct but are optional Edulytiks extensions. Independent teacher Cool-down 816÷34=24 is not copied from gated publisher materials.

KeyConcepts.Title: Complete exact verification
KeyConcepts.Definition: The sum of partial group counts plus any final remainder must reconstruct dividend.

Lessons.Title: Practice an Algorithm Using Partial Quotients
ExplanationParagraphs: Original IM 2021 Grade5 U04:L14 Practice an Algorithm Using Partial Quotients: the task is to SPOT AND EXPLAIN mathematical ERRORS in source learners' stacked division, then repair the whole-number quotient. Correct answers alone do not satisfy error diagnosis; some image labels conflict with computed partial products by design.

Warm-up Which One Doesn't Belong Different Ways: original source shows four written division layouts A–D. The HTML text includes a partially described 1312÷82 figure whose textual side label is ambiguous ('83' in the description), so do NOT infer or certify the full WODB diagrams from text alone. Teacher shows original images and accepts defensible distinctions.

Activity 1 Find the Mistake original example 1: source stack claims 1656÷46=29 and first removes 920 for 20 groups, then incorrectly reports remainder436. Correct first remainder 1656−920=736. Subsequent source subtraction positions are also inconsistent; exact quotient is 36 since 46×36=1656. Student must identify the wrong subtraction and explain a fully consistent repair, e.g. 46×30=1380 remainder276 then 46×6=276.
Activity 1 original example 2: source claims 972÷18=64 from '60' and '4' partials, but subtracts 900. Nine hundred is 50×18, NOT 60×18. Then 972−900=72 and72÷18=4, so correct quotient is 50+4=54.

Activity 1 original example 3: source claims 744÷24=211 but records subtracting 480, then240, then remainder24. 480=20×24, NOT 200×24; 240=10×24; 24=1×24. Correct quotient20+10+1=31, verified by31×24=744.

Activity 2 Practice Problems: source teacher HTML identifies four numberless diagram captions without independently readable operand values; preserve teacher-led completion of those printed problems and label any alternative exact exercises as original Edulytiks extras. Exact selected Practice supports three verified corrected quotients and source chunk calculations, but original handwritten error explanation remains TEACHER_REVIEW_REQUIRED. Independent Cool-down uses 1512÷42.

KeyConcepts.Title: Error diagnosis in partial quotients
KeyConcepts.Definition: A mistaken product or subtraction changes the remaining amount and can create false quotient claims.

KeyConcepts.Title: Use hundreds-sized chunks
KeyConcepts.Definition: For four-digit dividends, subtracting 100 or200 divisor groups at once may be more efficient.
KeyConcepts.Example: The remaining1815 is still divisible by33.

KeyConcepts.Title: Independent multiplication check
KeyConcepts.Definition: A valid exact quotient must reproduce the dividend when multiplied by the divisor.
KeyConcepts.Example: The final remainder must also be below the divisor.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Accept a plausible rounded partial product as exact
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Partial quotients require exact divisor multiples and exact subtraction.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Check each chosen chunk with multiplication before removing it.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Use only tens-sized chunks for every large dividend
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Small chunks may work but cause avoidable repetitive work for four-digit dividends.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Consider a 100- or 200-group chunk and verify it does not exceed the remainder.
